syllabus: NSW Studies of Religion II Stage 6 Syllabus, Preliminary (Year 11) course

units.title: The nature of religion and beliefs

points.title: The supernatural dimension
points.brief: Religions hold beliefs about a reality beyond the everyday world. Transcendent means a divine power beyond the world; immanent means one present within it.

points.title: The characteristics of religion
points.brief: Religions share features of beliefs, sacred texts and stories, ethics, and rituals and ceremonies, which work together as a whole.

points.title: The contribution of religion
points.brief: Religion gives individuals meaning, identity and guidance, and gives societies shared values, community and ways to mark life's stages.

points.title: The Dreaming
points.brief: For many Aboriginal peoples, the Dreaming is an ongoing reality that explains creation, law, kinship and connection to land, not only a time in the past.

points.title: Kinship, Country and identity
points.brief: In Aboriginal spiritualities, kinship sets each person's relationships and responsibilities, and Country is central to identity and spiritual life.

points.title: The origins of Buddhism
points.brief: Buddhism began in northern India about 2,500 years ago with Siddhartha Gautama, who became the Buddha, the awakened one.

points.title: The Four Noble Truths
points.brief: Life involves suffering (dukkha), suffering comes from craving, it can end, and the Eightfold Path is the way to end it.

points.title: Buddhist sacred texts
points.brief: Buddhist teachings are kept in texts such as the Pali Canon (Tipitaka), and schools such as Theravada and Mahayana value different collections.

points.title: Buddhist ethics
points.brief: The Five Precepts guide conduct, such as not harming living beings and not taking what is not given. Karma links actions to their results.

points.title: Buddhist practice
points.brief: Meditation, offerings at temples and honouring the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha are central to Buddhist life.

points.title: The origins of Christianity
points.brief: Christianity began in the first century CE with the followers of Jesus of Nazareth in Judea, and spread across the Roman Empire.

points.title: Principal Christian beliefs
points.brief: Christians believe in one God as Trinity (Father, Son and Holy Spirit), that Jesus is divine and human, and in his death and resurrection.

points.title: The Bible
points.brief: The Christian Bible holds the Hebrew scriptures, shared in part with Judaism, and the writings of the early church, including the four Gospels and the letters.

points.title: Christian ethics
points.brief: The Ten Commandments, the Beatitudes and Jesus's command to love God and your neighbour guide Christian ethics.

points.title: Christian worship and sacraments
points.brief: Christians gather for worship, often on Sundays. Many churches celebrate sacraments such as baptism and the Eucharist.

points.title: The origins of Hinduism
points.brief: Hinduism grew over thousands of years in the Indian subcontinent and has no single founder.

points.title: Principal Hindu beliefs
points.brief: Many Hindus believe in Brahman, the ultimate reality, in the cycle of rebirth (samsara) shaped by karma, and in liberation (moksha).

points.title: Hindu sacred texts
points.brief: Hindu texts include the Vedas, the Upanishads, and epics such as the Mahabharata, which contains the Bhagavad Gita.

points.title: Hindu ethics
points.brief: Dharma is right duty according to a person's stage of life and place in society. Ahimsa, non-violence, is a widely held value.

points.title: Hindu practice
points.brief: Puja, worship at home or in a temple, festivals such as Diwali, and pilgrimage are important forms of Hindu practice.

points.title: The origins of Islam
points.brief: Islam began in Arabia in the 7th century CE, when Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad received God's revelation.

points.title: Principal Islamic beliefs
points.brief: Muslims believe in one God (Allah), angels, the prophets with Muhammad the last, the revealed books, the Day of Judgement and God's decree.

points.title: The Quran and Hadith
points.brief: The Quran is the word of God revealed to Muhammad. The Hadith record the sayings and actions of the Prophet and guide practice.

points.title: The Five Pillars
points.brief: The declaration of faith (shahada), prayer five times a day (salat), giving to the poor (zakat), fasting in Ramadan (sawm) and pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj).

points.title: Islamic ethics
points.brief: Sharia, drawn from the Quran and Hadith, guides how Muslims live, and actions are judged as permitted or forbidden.

points.title: The origins of Judaism
points.brief: Judaism traces its origins to Abraham and the covenant with God, and to Moses receiving the Torah at Sinai.

points.title: Principal Jewish beliefs
points.brief: Jews believe in one God, the covenant between God and the Jewish people, and the importance of following God's commandments.

points.title: The Torah and the Tanakh
points.brief: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh. The Talmud records rabbinic teaching and discussion.

points.title: Jewish ethics
points.brief: The 613 commandments (mitzvot), including the Ten Commandments, and values such as justice and repairing the world guide Jewish life.

points.title: Jewish practice
points.brief: Observing the Sabbath (Shabbat) from Friday evening to Saturday evening, keeping kosher and festivals such as Passover are central practices.

points.title: The origins of Shinto
points.brief: Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, with roots in ancient Japanese beliefs and no single founder.

points.title: Kami
points.brief: Kami are spirits or sacred powers found in nature, places, ancestors and people of great achievement.

points.title: Shrines and rituals
points.brief: Worship takes place at shrines, marked by torii gates, through purification, offerings and prayers.

points.title: Purity in Shinto
points.brief: Shinto values purity and sincerity, and rituals of cleansing remove impurity before approaching the kami.

points.title: The effect of colonisation on Aboriginal spiritualities
points.brief: Dispossession separated many Aboriginal peoples from their land, kinship groups and ceremonies, which damaged the basis of their spiritual life.

points.title: The arrival of Christianity
points.brief: Christianity arrived with the First Fleet in 1788. The Church of England was dominant at first, with Catholic, Presbyterian and Methodist churches growing.

points.title: Sectarianism
points.brief: Tension between Catholics, many of Irish descent, and Protestants shaped Australian politics, schools and work into the 20th century.

points.title: Churches in Australian society
points.brief: Churches ran schools, hospitals and charities, and influenced laws on issues such as drinking and Sunday trading.

points.title: Other traditions before 1945
points.brief: Jewish communities, Muslim cameleers from Afghanistan and British India, and Chinese miners on the goldfields brought other traditions to Australia.
